lead: Paul gives thanks because the faith of the Thessalonians is growing and their love for one another increasing, even under persecution. In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven at the Last Supper and begins his great prayer: “Father, the hour has come.” He tells us what eternal life is: to know the Father, the only true God, and the one whom he has sent. The key words are growing and knowing.

set: 2 Thessalonians names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders. Many scholars think it was written later by a disciple in Paul's name, because its tone and its teaching about the Day of the Lord differ from 1 Thessalonians; others hold that Paul wrote it soon after the first letter, around AD 51. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture.

The church of Thessalonica was still suffering persecution. Some members were also confused about the Lord's coming, thinking that the Day of the Lord had already come (2:2). The letter opens, as Paul's letters usually do, with thanksgiving, and here the thanksgiving is also encouragement.
str: v. 3: thanksgiving for growing faith and increasing love.
v. 4: Paul boasts of their steadfastness among the churches.
vv. 5–7: their sufferings are a sign of God's just judgment; relief will come when the Lord Jesus is revealed.
kw: A rare compound verb, found only here in the New Testament: “grows beyond measure”. Faith is alive. It is meant to grow, like a plant that has taken root.
Not passive endurance but staying power: remaining under a weight without giving way. Paul names it together with faith, as the fruit that persecution has not destroyed.
The Lord's coming is described as an unveiling. Christ is already Lord; at the end his glory, now hidden, will be seen by all.
vv: because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing.
In 1 Thessalonians Paul had prayed that their love would increase (1 Thessalonians 3:12). Now he sees the prayer answered.
Therefore we ourselves boast of you among the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith during all your persecutions and the afflictions that you are enduring.
Paul tells other churches about them. The witness of one suffering community strengthens the whole Church.
This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, and is intended to make you worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering.
Their suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned them. It is a sign that they belong to his kingdom, which the world resists.
and to give relief to the afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven
Justice belongs to God, not to us. Paul elsewhere tells believers never to avenge themselves but to leave room for God (Romans 12:19). In the POC, verses 6 and 7 are arranged in a different order.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a word of hope for those who suffer for the faith. The Catechism teaches that on the last day Christ will come in glory to bring about the definitive triumph of good over evil, and that the Last Judgment will reveal that God's justice triumphs over all the injustices committed by his creatures (CCC 681, 1040). We pray for Christians who suffer in many lands, and for those who wrong them, leaving all judgment to the Lord.

set: John 17 is the long prayer of Jesus at the end of the Last Supper, just before he goes out to the garden where he will be arrested (18:1). Since the sixteenth century it has often been called the “priestly prayer”, because in it Jesus consecrates himself and offers himself to the Father for his disciples (17:19).

Throughout John's Gospel “the hour” has been coming: at Cana it “has not yet come” (2:4); at the feast his enemies could not arrest him, “because his hour had not yet come” (7:30). In 12:23 Jesus says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Now, in prayer, he hands that hour to the Father.
str: v. 1: the hour has come: glorify your Son, that the Son may glorify you.
v. 2: the Son's authority, to give eternal life.
v. 5: the glory he had with the Father before the world existed.
kw: Not sixty minutes, but the decisive time set by the Father: the hour of the cross, the resurrection and the return to the Father, seen as one.
In the Old Testament God's glory is his presence made visible. In John, the glory of Jesus is revealed above all on the cross, where his love goes to the end (13:1).
The verb is in a form that speaks of continuing knowledge. In the Bible to know is not only to have information but to be in a living relationship, as husband and wife know each other.
vv: After Jesus had spoken these words, he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you,
Jesus prays with his eyes lifted up, as he did at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). The first word is “Father”, the word on which the whole prayer rests.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Eternal life is not only endless time after death. It begins now, in knowing God. Many commentators think the wording here, with the full name “Jesus Christ”, reflects the evangelist's own confession of faith.
I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.
On the cross Jesus will say, “It is finished” (19:30). The work is the Father's will, carried out to the end.
So now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had in your presence before the world existed.
The Son existed with the Father before creation, as the prologue says: “In the beginning was the Word” (1:1). The Church confesses this in the Creed: “God from God, Light from Light”.
ch: The Catechism calls this the prayer of the hour of Jesus, rightly named his “priestly” prayer, which takes in the whole economy of creation and salvation, his death and resurrection (CCC 2746–2751). Verse 3 is often quoted in Christian teaching to show that the goal of our life is communion with God. In every Holy Qurbono we are drawn into this prayer, as the priest lifts the gifts and our hearts to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

qa: Does “the only true God” mean that Jesus is not God?

No. Jesus contrasts the one true God with the false gods of the nations, and in the same breath names himself as the one sent, whom to know is eternal life. Two verses later he speaks of the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed” (17:5). The Church has always read this prayer as the Son speaking to the Father in the unity of the one God (CCC 240–242).
study: Paul thanks God that the love of the Thessalonians “for one another is increasing”. How could love grow in my own home this week?
Jesus says eternal life is to know the Father and the one he has sent. What helps me to know him and not only to know about him?
